Title: New card to "fix" the weenie problem

Messages.Author: Damnans
Messages.Body:
I have been thinking about a way for high capacity vampires to deal
with weenies in the early game without adding new rules to the game,
and this is the card I came up with:

Card Name: Insert cool name here
Cardtype: Master
Cost: 0
Requires at least 2 vampires with a capacity above 7 in your
uncontrolled region. Only playable if you control no minions.
Put this card in play and put 3 counters on it. If there are any
counters on this card and you control no minions, you do not burn pool
either for being bled or for the effects of a referendum. Remove a
counter on this card during your discard phase. Tap this card to
discard a copy of this card in your hand to move a minion card in your
ash heap to the bottom of your library. A Methuselah can only play one
copy of this card per game.

--

>discard a copy of this card in your hand to move a minion card in your
>ash heap to the bottom of your library. A Methuselah can only play one
>copy of this card per game.

I'm not a fan, for various reasons.

1) Seven Line Syndrome. The card is long and wordy.

2) This card needs to be played turn 1 or 2, really. There's little
benefit to playing it much later than that, for its intended purpose.
So you have to stuff your deck with 10 of them. (Compare Info Highway,
which can have significant positive late-game benefits for fatties using
Govern, or to speedily bring out a vampire following an oust.) That's a
lot of your deck being given over to 1 card that is mostly only intended
for turn 1 or 2.

3) Though on the flipside, one seemingly incidental effect of this card
is holding it as a blocker strategy when you get pwned by a weenie
combat deck, or similar. Throw it down when they burn Etrius, and they
may have trouble bleeding you. I'm not sure that's either intentional
or positive.

4) Though it harms weenie decks, clearly, it also hurts a number of
other decks that probably don't need to be toned down. For example,
bruise-bleed decks often capitalize on being able to get bleeds through
when the opportunity arises. They can't go into combat with you (no
minions), they can't bleed you. Sit on their hands. Ditto, midcap
bleed or whatever. They're decks you could reasonably try to fend off.

Elsewhere, someone came up with the idea of having crypt cards that gave
you extra transfers, which is quite a neat idea. Extending that...

Making An Example
Artwork: Some thin-blood being hanged, or set fire to, or
something.
Crypt card back, but with a library card front that looks a bit
like The Embrace etc.
1 capacity, clanless Independent vampire
When this card is in play, it is a unique master card. If you
have controlled Making An Example before, burn this card. Put 3
counters on it when it enters play, and remove a counter during
your untap phase. Burn it if it has no counters. When vampires
of less than 4 capacity or minions with a cost less than 4 bleed
you or call referendums, you neither gain nor lose pool as a
result of that action if you control no minions.

Which is still a bit awkward on the SLS front, but might be an
interesting twist on the whole problem. I mind losing the crypt space
less, because it's a fattie deck which typically bring out only a few
vampires, rather than sacrificing 8-12 cards from your library.

It still leaves the late game awkwardness. Include it to fend people
off when you're dying. I'm not sure.

I initially thought about having it remove all copies of itself from the
game too. But actually, I rather like having the ability for you to
have 4 copies of Arika, 2 Queen Anne, 2 Lucinde, 4 Making An Examples,
and have some crypt construction problems to tweak. Sort of like a star
vampire deck, only different.

(Disclaimer: my own work, White Wolf welcome to use/adapt/borrow etc.)

--

"Main problem" to you may be cumulative actions on turn 10, but it
seems that to these people, "main problem" refers to actions taken
before Arika can act.

I personally feel the 20 conditioning or 20 KRC or 40 Computer Hacking
etc. is the most scary type of weenie deck, but it seems to be the
least prevalent, so I don't think it needs nurfing.

I don't think most build-to-a-crescendo weenies (i.e. your boon-based
decks) need any real nurfing.

So, what does?

This doesn't matter to anyone reading this thread, however, because
this would be attempting to identify the problem. I have tried to do
this in previous threads and it does not seem anyone who suggests a
solution to this "problem" wants to /identify/ the problem.

I am pretty unconvinced that anything will be done about this until
somebody takes the time to say something other than "look how many
actions they have"; real results will have to come into it. Weenies
worked great in the past, and still work great in theory--but in
practise, they just get killed by Ancilla Empowerment, or Howler, or
table hate, or whatever.

If a real problem is pointed out, I think LSJ will give us a real
solution. Until then, I doubt anyone is listening.

-- Brian

I think this thread points out that the problem is bad deck building.
People want to ignore capacity considerations and build decks with
FIVE copies of a vampire that takes 3 turns to transfer out. They
don't want to use lots of Dreams/InfoHighway/Zillah's Valley/Tomb of
Ramses or even Dummy Corporation to make up for this. They think
Effective Management is only for weenie decks, and not to improve your
selection from the varied spread of vampires with different levels of
your chosen disciplines and clans that you have put in your crypt to
play the cards you put in your library.
They don't want to take advantage of their high capacity vampires with
lots of Minion Taps, backed up by Giants Blood or Entrenching or Voter
Captivation or Golconda.

Really, the only reason to not play with some 1caps and 3caps and 5
caps in your deck is because you want to bring out a big vamp and put
a Soul Gem and a skill card on them. If you're tapping into that level
of power, you deserve an associated risk of being in front of a quick
starter. If they are playing only high cap vamps and not moving them
out quickly and using them to bloat, then they deserve to die because
they have overtransferred -- stretched out their influence beyond its
reasonable limits -- piddled away their resources.

Basic deckbuilding from the first release of this game included using
vampires with a range of capacities. It was practically built in when
you got your first set of cards, because you had a limited
collection.

Actually, you'd be surprised just how significant a problem Seven Line
Syndrome can be. Not for all players or all play-groups, of course.
But there are a number of people whose eyes will glaze over once a card
hits too much text.

Fata Amria is a good example, here.

>> 2) This card needs to be played turn 1 or 2, really. There's little
>> benefit to playing it much later than that, for its intended purpose.
>> So you have to stuff your deck with 10 of them. (Compare Info Highway,

I see you're jumping to conclusions.

>since the card already
>addresses that problem you mention:
>
>Relevant text: "Tap this card to discard a copy of this card in your
>hand to move a minion card in your ash heap to the bottom of your
>library."

I think it's little more than a sticking plaster for a nasty design
feature.

There are a few strands going on here.

1) You need 8-12 copies in a deck. There is, essentially, no point
putting the card in a deck *at all* unless you put sufficient in to make
it come up first two turns. Which is a bit icky. Compare Info Highway.
People often put 2-4 copies in decks, and mix and match with Dreams of
the Sphinx. If either of them come up early, great! Free transfers,
Arika comes out a touch quicker than otherwise, or you can start on the
next vampire a little quicker. Whichever. If they turn up in the late
game, that's fine too because the cards still have a positive use. So
you can make a deliberate strategic choice. Should I put in quite a
few? Can I cope with one or two? This card doesn't allow that. It
basically says "You must put 10 of me in a deck."

2) Land. When Garfield created Jyhad, he didn't want to replicate the
mistake of land. There shouldn't be the need for a huge hunk of cards
in your deck that's basically only there to let you do other stuff. A
huge hunk of these feels very similar to that.

3) Sticking plaster. Even a fatty deck can make some very rapid
advances in terms of numbers of cards used. Multi-acting decks, or
throwing everything it's got at a given action. This can be multiple
cards. Pulling into your card is pulling into dead weight, and clumping
can mean they easily pull multiples (either through poor shuffling,
because humans are bad at it, or just statistical tomfoolery). If I
can't get rid of all of them, what do I do? Hold them to use next turn,
clogging my hand? Discard them normally, as the dead weight they are?

You might get a somewhat easier solution by making it burn option, and
including a line like "You may discard <foo> from your hand using the
Burn Option rules if you have one in play already."

>> 4) Though it harms weenie decks, clearly, it also hurts a number of
>> other decks that probably don't need to be toned down. For example,
>> bruise-bleed decks often capitalize on being able to get bleeds through
>> when the opportunity arises. They can't go into combat with you (no
>> minions), they can't bleed you. Sit on their hands. Ditto, midcap
>> bleed or whatever. They're decks you could reasonably try to fend off.
>
>Well, that would only happen for 3 turns. But in any case, playtesting
>should fix the problems that arise with the use of this card (or cards
>alike).

The point being that bruise-bleed decks, amongst others, capitalize on
the gaps in their prey's defences. No minions? Quick, nip in with a
couple of bleed. No combat defence? A quick rush. Hybrid strategies
generally do this sort of thing. Making it quite as blanket as you have
means that there's a lot of collateral damage.



Along those lines, (and I think I've suggested this before at some
point), it seems like the game may have benefitted from a balance
standpoint if there were 3 levels of disciplines instead of 2 (also
from a thematic stand point because really the idea that Chandler
Hungerford would be as Protelicious as Stanislava is laughable).

Seeing as how it's probably too late to introduce a third discipline
level to the game, I'm not sure why the following design tactic isn't
implemented (more, if it has been at all):

Over the Hill
1 Blood
[pot] Strike for 1R
[POT] Strike for 2R. If the striking vampire's capacity is greater
than 8, then the strike is for 3R and costs one less blood.

Seems simple and elegant enough (provided that we don't do this with
cards that already have too much card text) and it just may help
address Gines' point.

Peteo

doesn't reliably wins you games.

Brian Moritz wrote:
> "Main problem" to you may be cumulative actions on turn 10, but it

I should have re-phrased that. For me, the problem I see is that
the action (or reaction) of a large-cap vampire (with a few
exceptions) is not worth sufficiently more than a vampire of lower
capacity (weenie, midcap, whatever). A smaller vampire can generate
almost as much intercept, almost as much stealth, almost as much
bleed, almost as much strength, etc. At the same time, there's
definitely an upper boundary from a design perspective on how much
pool should be lost during a single action, so it's hard to justify
giving large-cap vampires a proportionate ability to inflict pool loss
per action. Still, I think a lot more can be done to improve the
quality of the actions of large-caps. Hell, it'd be nice to see a top-
tier rush deck that wasn't a weenie deck.

- Ben Peal

How's this for a variant:

Untapping "as normal" costs an influence.

Details:
It doesn't really "cost" an influence, since you don't have influence
to spend during your untap phase. Rather, when untapping your minions,
you note how many you untapped "as normal" (the ones that were already
untapped don't count for this). Call it X. Then, during your influence
phase, your number of transfers is reduced by X. If X is greater than
your transfers, you get zero transfers and must make up the excess
with pool or blood (or life), no more than 1 blood/life per minion.

Can be combined with the 5+1 transfer variant:
http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/78c7f3b44ad46b4f

>with pool or blood (or life), no more than 1 blood/life per minion.

I'm mildly concerned about the knock-on effects to a few things,
notably:

- "pay one to see one", in the mid-game or late-game, or even in the
early game for a bad shuffle on a star vampire deck which has
weenies but isn't really a weenie deck. Playing your deck (i.e.
untapping vampires) causes it to be more expensive to draw
vampires in the late game, and bringing out one or two weenies
for early defence against a really bad shuffle of a star-vampire
deck may leave you in a sticky situation.

- advancement becomes harder. Though Gift of Experience and Epiphany
both exist to merge vampires outside of the influence phase,
this - like pay one to see one - becomes more expensive. I'm
not sure merging vampires should be harder.

- does it make Inconnu Tutelage a bit too expensive for others to use?
One of the nice balancing effects of Inconnu Tutelage, to my
mind, is that it gives everyone else the possibility to use it
without too much bother, once they hit the mid-game. Since
they'd be using up their transfers, it becomes more bothersome
to use for other players. The player using it can, of course,
be doing things like using Info Highway to try to counteract
this, whereas the other players now have to make extra effort.

Oh, I wasn't trying to invalidate the basic idea. But it seems silly
not to raise concerns when they might prompt someone (you, me, someone
else on the group, a canny playtester in private or at an unofficial
tournament you run, whoever) to come up with a better suggestion that
could be playtested thoroughly.

Re-reading the mechanism: if I have 4 vampires out, untap all, costing 4
transfers, can I get any transfers at all in my influence phase? Or is
it only that I burn for the number of minions untapped "as normal" in
excess of 4? (Or whatever number my transfers are.) Basically, if I
have 4 vampires out and no other transfer-altering effects for the rest
of the game, do I have zero transfers for the rest of the game? Or can
I burn blood to buy them back?

Another concern I had about this today goes as follows. Same situation
as above - comment, not invalidation.

Assume I have two vampires out (reasonable) and I'm playing Govern the
Unaligned at superior. Which seems a not unreasonable setup. Two
vampires untapping costs two transfers.[0] My vamp plays Govern the
Unaligned. I have two transfers left. Depending on the answer to the
question above, I either have to bring it back over three turns (2
transfers spare each turn) or I'd need to burn two extra blood to "buy"
two more transfers to bring two pool back. Alternatively, I have to
draw the blood back slowly. Or I have to play Info Highway, or Ingrid
Rossler, or something.

If I have 3 or 4 vampires out (3 midcaps, 4-7, isn't that unreasonable),
this becomes a lot more problematic!

Now, this might be sort of a good thing with Govern the Unaligned, which
a lot of people would like to see toned down in power. And it might be
okay for Enchant Kindred. But I would be less happy about it hitting,
say, Ecoterrorists or Reunion Kamut, both of which exist to fill pool
gain gaps, IMO.

And because those pool gain mechanisms would suffer, would it make Blood
Doll, Minion Tap, Grooming the Protege, and Information Highway (and
friends) commensurately more necessary (even more necessary, perhaps),
which would make some of the really nice master cards that exist for
things *other than* pool gain vanish. Which would seem to be a pity.

A tangential thought: one of the major sources of potential pool gain
comes from this. Church of Vindicated Faith, Inspire, and Travis being
the obvious cards for this sort of thing, obviously. Many of the
alternatives available to vampires - Blood Doll etc. - are not available
to Imbued. (Info Highway is, of course.)

Again, people might like this sort of thing, though.

[0] I also think it would be easier to just give players their transfers
at the start of the turn, in this setup.
